newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican sugar industry fears corn syrup invasion.
newsitem.headline: Mexican sugar industry fears corn syrup invasion.

text.p: Mexico's sugar industry, having achieved record harvests of over 4.4 million tonnes for the past three cycles, now fears its efforts could be wasted by an invasion of corn syrup sweetners, sources said Monday.

The threat from high fructose corn syrup (HFCS), both domestic production and imports from the United States, looms large, especially given Mexico's high consumption of soft drinks, the most frequently applied use for HFCSs.

A director of the National Sugar Chamber, the body that groups the country's mill owners, estimated that imports of corn syrup this year could rise to 500,000 tonnes from the approximate 350,000 tonnes imported during 1996.
Such is the concern of the HFCS threat that the chamber director predicted the closure of between 20 and 30 mills next cycle as corn sweetners replace traditional sugars. Mexico has 61 active mills.

"The objective of corn syrup producers is to snap up the entire soft drink industry which currently consumes around 1.5 million tonnes of sugar per year," the chamber director said, requesting anonimity.

"We calculate that between 20 and 30 of the mills currently operating, mainly the small ones, are the most vulnerable to closure," he said, adding that price competition from corn syrup would bring the pressures.

Enrique Molina, chairman of Consorcio Azucarero Escorpion, the country's largest sugar company with nine mills, told Reforma newspaper he estimates that corn syrup imports would hit 500,000 tonnes this year.

Molina added the sweetner would directly displace around 500,000 tonnes of sugar. He calculated Mexico's excess production this year at 300,000 tonnes, meaning possible exports in the region of 800,000 tonnes from the 96-97 crop which is currently winding down.

One sugar industrialist, who declined to be named, said the figure of 20-30 closures was exaggerated but said that the worries that corn syrup would continue to eat into sugar market share were very real.
According to his figures, corn syrup had just five percent of the Mexican sweetner market in 1995 and 11 percent in 1996. "It could easily go to 16 to 18 percent this year," he added.

"Our recent efforts to increase sugar production, largely through productivity, could go to waste if HFCSs gain more ground. A balance has to be found," he added, although he recognised it was a tangled political web.
The chamber is currently awaiting a decision of a government investigation of alleged corn syrup dumping at prices below cost that mill owners have brought against HFCS importers.

Mexico also has two HFCS production facilities in operation. Arancia Corn Products, a joint venture between Arancia and CPC International, has a 18,000 tonnes per month plant on line in the city of Queretaro, with plans to boost production to 60,000 tonner per month in the future.
Almidones Mexicanos (Almex) also has a corn syrup production venture with Tate & Lyle in the western city of Guadalajara.
One factor in the sugar-syrup battle that annoys Mexican sugar industrialists is that the nation has to import the type of corn needed to be processed in syrup plants.

"What we want is a level playing field. We think it only right that HFCS production in Mexico uses Mexican-grown corn," Jose Pinto Mazal, director of mill owners Beta San Miguel and a leading light in the national chamber, told Reuters recently.

Industrialists also claim that U.S. farming subsidies allow corn syrup industries to produce the sweetner at prices up to 30 percent cheaper than Mexican sugar, which, even with freight costs, allow them to undercut local sugar prices.

Mexico's sugar harvest, entering its final phases for this 1996-1997 cycle, had produced 4,495,663 tonnes to June 14, according to the Agroindustry Sugar Committee that oversees output throughout the crop cycle.
